title: Potentiometer and its applications
notes: The applications all use the same null. Comparing two cells uses E1/E2 = l1/l2. Measuring a thermocouple's small emf uses a small potential gradient so that the balance length is long enough to read.

Internal resistance uses two balance lengths. l1 is with the cell alone. l2 is with a known resistance R across the cell, so the cell now sends current and its terminal voltage is smaller. Then r = R (l1/l2 − 1).
A standard cell of known emf can set k. If that cell balances at l_s, then k = E_s / l_s, and an unknown balanced at l has E = k l. The standard cell must not be left on load.

Sensitivity improves when k is small, because a small change in emf moves the jockey a long way. That means a long wire or a small driving current, until the galvanometer can no longer see the unbalance.
The wire must stay uniform and at one temperature. A jockey scraped along a hot wire both damages the wire and shifts k.
The positive terminal of the test cell goes toward the high-potential end of the wire. Reversed terminals give no balance point.
